claim: Four male Long-Evans rats weighing 500–700 g (~6–12 months old) were used in this study.
source: Four male Long-Evans rats weighing 500–700 g (~6–12 months old) were used in this study.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing the subjects.

claim: Rats were housed in custom-made acrylic cages (40 cm × 40 cm × 40 cm) on a reverse light cycle (Light: 8:00 pm to 8:00 am).
source: Rats were housed in custom-made acrylic cages (40 cm × 40 cm × 40 cm) on a reverse light cycle (Light: 8:00 pm to 8:00 am).
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing housing conditions.

claim: 488 place cells were included with place field distributed on the circular track but not located at the resting box.
source: In this study, 488 place cells were included with place field distributed on the circular track but not located at the resting box.
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section describing the dataset.

claim: 120 (24.6%) out of 488 cells were significantly phase-locked to gamma rhythms.
source: We employed local LFPs as reference to detect gamma phase-locking and found that 120 (24.6%) out of these cells were significantly phase-locked to gamma rhythms, a majority of which (113 cells, 23.2%) exhibited significant phase-locking to fast gamma rhythms (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 2C and supplementary figures showing the analysis results.

claim: 113 cells (23.2%) exhibited significant phase-locking to fast gamma rhythms.
source: We employed local LFPs as reference to detect gamma phase-locking and found that 120 (24.6%) out of these cells were significantly phase-locked to gamma rhythms, a majority of which (113 cells, 23.2%) exhibited significant phase-locking to fast gamma rhythms (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 2C and supplementary figures.

claim: A very small number (3.7%) of cells were found to phase-locked to slow gamma rhythms.
source: However, a very small number (3.7%) of cells were found to phase-locked to slow gamma rhythms.
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section.

claim: The preferred fast gamma phases of FG-cells (202.38 ± 2.01°) were concentrated around the peak of fast gamma cycle.
source: Their preferred fast gamma phases (202.38 ± 2.01°) were concentrated around the peak of fast gamma cycle, which was consistent with the findings in Schomburg et al., 2014.
evidence: Directly stated with citation to previous work (Schomburg et al., 2014).

claim: The fast gamma phase-locking of FG-cells was stable across trials, with a significantly higher mean vector length of fast gamma phase-locking than those of NFG-cells.
source: Furthermore, the fast gamma phase-locking of FG-cells was stable across trials, with a significantly higher mean vector length of fast gamma phase-locking than those of NFG-cells (Figure 2D, repeated measure ANOVA, main effect of cell type, F(1,22) = 33.9, p = 7.5 × 10–6, partial η2 = 0.6; main effect of trials, F(4,88) = 1.3, p = 0.3, partial η2 = 0.06, no cell type × trials interaction, F(4,88) = 0.5, p = 0.8, partial η2 = 0.02).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical analysis results and reference to Figure 2D.

claim: A larger proportion of neurons in FG-cells had significant theta phase precession than NFG-cell.
source: Meanwhile, we also found that a larger proportion of neurons in FG-cells had significant theta phase precession than NFG-cell (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Chi-squared test, ratio of theta phase precession cell among the FG- vs. NFG-cell, n = 457 cell，χ2 = 13.7, p = 2.1 × 10–4, Cramer V = 0.2).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical analysis and reference to supplementary figure.

claim: The weighted correlation of theta sequences decoded by excluding FG-cells spikes (exFG-sequences) was much lower than that of theta sequences decoded by excluding downsampled NFG-cells spikes (exNFG-sequences) in the same theta cycles.
source: We found that the weighted correlation of theta sequences decoded by excluding FG-cells spikes (exFG-sequences) was much lower than that of theta sequences decoded by excluding downsampled NFG-cells spikes (exNFG-sequences) in the same theta cycles (Figure 3C, generalized linear mixed model, main effect of cell type, F(2,7255) = 53.0, p = 0; post hoc test, raw sequences vs. exFG-sequences, p = 0, raw sequences vs. exNFG-sequences, p = 4.6 × 10–8, exFG-sequences vs. exNFG-sequences, p = 1.1 × 10–6).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 3C.

claim: The sequential structure could be dominantly interrupted by excluding FG-cells rather than NFG-cells.
source: This suggests that the sequential structure could be dominantly interrupted by excluding FG-cells rather than NFG-cells.
evidence: Inference drawn from the weighted correlation analysis results.

claim: The development of theta sequences along with exploration experience was observed.
source: Consistent with the previous studies (Feng et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2020), we also observed the development of theta sequences along with exploration experience (Figure 3D, E, repeated measure ANOVA, main effect of trials, F(4,44) = 7.0, p = 2.0 × 10–4, partial η2 = 0.4).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical analysis, reference to previous studies (Feng et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2020), and Figure 3D, E.

claim: The rats were running at stable running speed and head direction across trials.
source: This could not be accounted for by behavioral parameters, as the rats were running at stable running speed and head direction across trials (Figure 3F, repeated measure ANOVA, main effect of trials: F(4,44) = 0.9, p = 0.5, partial η2 = 0.07; Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Watson–Williams multi-sample test, F(4,55) = 0.2, p = 0.9, partial η2 = 0.01).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 3F and supplementary figure.

claim: The temporospatial structure of the theta sequences cannot be developed with experience when the FG-cell spikes were excluded.
source: Interestingly, the temporospatial structure of the theta sequences cannot be developed with experience when the FG-cell spikes were excluded, with significantly lower weighted correlation than theta sequences constructed by excluding NFG-cell spikes (Figure 3D, G, repeated measure ANOVA, trials × cell type interaction, F(4,44) = 3.0, p = 0.03, partial η2 = 0.2, main effect of cell type, F(1,11) = 7.8, p = 0.02, partial η2 = 0.4; main effect of trials, F(4,44) = 4.0, p = 0.008).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 3D, G.

claim: During early development, the weighted correlation of both exFG- and exNFG-sequences was low.
source: We found that the weighted correlation of both exFG- and exNFG-sequences was low during early development (Figure 3H, paired t-test, t(24) = 0.2, p = 0.9, Cohen's d = 0.04).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 3H.

claim: During late development, the weighted correlation of exNFG-sequences was higher than that of exFG-sequences.
source: During late development, however, the weighted correlation of exNFG-sequences was higher than that of exFG-sequences (Figure 3H, paired t-test, t(24) = −3.7, p = 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.8).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 3H.

claim: The sweeping-ahead structure of the theta sequence was significantly disrupted when excluding a high percentage (~35%) of FG-cells during late development.
source: During late development, however, the sweeping-ahead structure of the theta sequence was significantly disrupted when excluding a high percentage (~35%) of FG-cells, which was not observed when excluding a low percentage (~10%) of FG-cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: The weighted correlation difference was close to 0 regardless of the fraction of excluded cells during early development.
source: The results showed that the weighted correlation difference was close to 0 regardless of the fraction of excluded cells during early development (Figure 4C, Pearson's correlation, Corr = 0.1, p = 0.7).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 4C.

claim: During late development, the weighted correlation difference was positively correlated with the fraction of excluded cells.
source: During late development, however, we found that the weighted correlation difference was positively correlated with the fraction of excluded cells (Figure 4D, Pearson's correlation, Corr = 0.6, p = 0.03).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 4D.

claim: The place fields of both FG- and NFG-cells could cover the entire track uniformly.
source: We found that although these two types of cells took different proportion of all recorded place cells, the place fields of both types of cells could cover the entire track uniformly (Figures 2C and 5A).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figures 2C and 5A.

claim: Similar distribution of place field COM between FG-cells and NFG-cells was found.
source: We measured the distribution of center of mass (COM) of main place field of FG-cells and number-matched NFG-cells (Figure 5B) and found similar distribution of place field COM between cell types (Figure 5C, two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, Z = 0.1, p = 0.8).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: The mean firing rate of FG-cell was significantly higher than NFG-cell.
source: Furthermore, Although the mean firing rate of FG-cell was significantly higher than NFG-cell (Figure 5D, Student's t-test, t(22) = 2.1, p = 0.04, Cohen's d = 0.9), the theta sequences in the above analyses were decoded by excluding similar numbers of spikes from FG- and NFG-cells (Figure 5E, excluded spike counts, t(22) = 1.2, p = 0.3, Cohen's d = 0.5), indicating that the different development patterns between exFG- and exNFG-sequences were not due to quality difference between two decoders.
evidence: Directly stated with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: The theta sequences were decoded by excluding similar numbers of spikes from FG- and NFG-cells.
source: Furthermore, Although the mean firing rate of FG-cell was significantly higher than NFG-cell (Figure 5D, Student's t-test, t(22) = 2.1, p = 0.04, Cohen's d = 0.9), the theta sequences in the above analyses were decoded by excluding similar numbers of spikes from FG- and NFG-cells (Figure 5E, excluded spike counts, t(22) = 1.2, p = 0.3, Cohen's d = 0.5), indicating that the different development patterns between exFG- and exNFG-sequences were not due to quality difference between two decoders.
evidence: Directly stated with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 5E.

claim: The two types of cells exhibited similar place fields size.
source: The two type of cells exhibited similar place fields size (Figure 5F), t(22) = 0.7, p = 0.5, Cohen's d = 0.3 and spatial information (Figure 5G) t(22) = 1.0, p = 0.3, Cohen's d = 0.4.
evidence: Directly stated with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 5F and 5G.

claim: The two types of cells exhibited similar spatial information.
source: The two type of cells exhibited similar place fields size (Figure 5F), t(22) = 0.7, p = 0.5, Cohen's d = 0.3 and spatial information (Figure 5G) t(22) = 1.0, p = 0.3, Cohen's d = 0.4.
evidence: Directly stated with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 5G.

claim: The slow gamma phases significantly shifted across successive slow gamma cycles.
source: By detecting the slow gamma phases of spikes within all theta cycles, we observed that the slow gamma phases significantly shifted across successive slow gamma cycles (Figure 6A, multi-sample Mardia–Watson–Wheeler test, W(4) = 369.4, p < 2.2 × 10–16; post hoc test, Cycle –1 vs. Cycle 0, W(2) = 97.5, p < 2.2 × 10–16, Cycle 0 vs. Cycle 1, W(2) = 95.4, p < 2.2 × 10–16), which was consistent with the previous finding (Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical analysis, reference to Figure 6A, and citation to previous work (Zheng et al., 2016).

claim: Slow gamma phase shifting, but not phase precession, was observed across successive gamma cycles during early development.
source: Interestingly, we observed slow gamma phase shifting, but not phase precession, across successive gamma cycles during early development. The distribution of slow gamma phases in Cycle 0 was similar as that in Cycle –1, then was dispersed in Cycle 1 (Figure 6B, multi-sample Mardia–Watson–Wheeler test, W(4) = 18.5, p = 9.8 × 10–4; post hoc test, Cycle –1 vs. Cycle 0, W(2) = 0.8, p = 0.7; Cycle 0 vs. Cycle 1, W(2) = 15.5, p = 4.4 × 10–4).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 6B.

claim: The slow gamma phase precession existed during late development.
source: However, the slow gamma phase precession existed during late development (Figure 6C, multi-sample Mardia–Watson–Wheeler test, W(4) = 21.2, p = 2.8 × 10–4; post hoc test, Cycle –1 vs Cycle 0, W(2) = 8.8, p = 0.01; Cycle 0 vs. Cycle 1, W(2) = 8.2, p = 0.02).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 6C.

claim: Slow gamma phase difference was significantly lower than 0 between two active slow gamma cycles.
source: We found that slow gamma phase difference was significantly lower than 0 between two active slow gamma cycles (Figure 7B, t-test, t(11) = −8.8, p = 2.6 × 10–6, Cohen's d = 5.3), as well as among 3 or ≥4 active slow gamma cycles for strict limitation of theta sequences modulated by slow gamma (3 active cycles, t(11) = −7.3, p = 1.5 × 10–5, Cohen's d = 4.4; ≥4 active cycles, t(8) = −3.6, p = 0.007, Cohen's d = 2.5).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 7B.

claim: In the first lap, the slow gamma phase differences were not significantly different from their surrogate data.
source: In the first lap, we found that the slow gamma phase differences were not significantly different from their surrogate data (Figure 7C, median of phase difference from lap1 was in 95% confidence intervals of those from shuffled data, p = 0.3).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 7C.

claim: The distribution of slow gamma phase difference was negatively biased compared with their surrogate data from lap2 onwards.
source: However, the distribution of slow gamma phase difference was negatively biased compared with their surrogate data (Figure 7C, median of phase difference from lap2–5 was beyond the 95% confidence intervals of those from shuffled data; lap2 p = 0.001, lap3 p = 0.001, lap4 p = 0.002, lap5 p = 0.002).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 7C.

claim: The slow gamma phase difference of FG-cells consistently exhibited a stable phase precession across trials, independent with learning experience.
source: We found that the slow gamma phase difference of FG-cells consistently exhibited a stable phase precession across trials, independent with learning experience (Figure 7E, lap1 p = 0.007, lap2 p = 0.006, lap3 p = 0.007, lap4 p = 0.002, lap5 p = 0.02).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 7E.

claim: The slow gamma phase precession of NFG-cells was experience dependent, with negative biased distribution of phase difference occurring from lap2.
source: In contrast, the slow gamma phase precession of NFG-cells was experience dependent, with negative biased distribution of phase difference occurring from lap2 (Figure 7E, lap1 p = 0.9, lap2 p = 0.01, lap3 p = 0.001, lap4 p = 0.009, lap5 p = 0.1).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 7E.

claim: Most data were distributed in the Quadrant1 (Q1) compared to the shuffled data distributed at the center.
source: Interestingly, we found most data were distributed in the Quadrant1 (Q1) compared to the shuffled data distributed at the center (Figure 8A, B).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 8A and 8B.

claim: The theta sequences with negative slow gamma phase difference and positive weighted correlation were significantly dominant.
source: The theta sequences with negative slow gamma phase difference and positive weighted correlation were significantly dominant (Figure 8C, the probability of observed data from lap1 exceeded 95% confidence intervals of those from shuffled data, p = 0.001).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 8C.

claim: The distribution of FG-cell sequences was significantly biased to Q1 than that of the shuffled data, not only in late development when the theta sequences have been developed, but also in early development.
source: Importantly, the distribution of FG-cell sequences was significantly biased to Q1 than that of the shuffled data, not only in late development when the theta sequences have been developed, but also in early development (Figure 8D–F, early development, p = 0.001; late development, p = 0.004).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 8D-F.

claim: For NFG-cell sequences, their distribution was significantly biased to Q1 than that of the shuffled data only in late development.
source: However, for NFG-cell sequences, their distribution was significantly biased to Q1 than that of the shuffled data only in late development (Figure 8G–I, bottom, p = 0.046), but not in early development (Figure 8G–I, top, p = 0.08).
evidence: Directly stated with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 8G-I.

claim: The hippocampus is known as its central role in encoding and storing experience and thus is essential for forming episodic memories.
source: The hippocampus is known as its central role in encoding and storing experience and thus is essential for forming episodic memories (Buzsáki et al., 2022; Cohen and Eichenbaum, 1993).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous work (Buzsáki et al., 2022; Cohen and Eichenbaum, 1993).

claim: Hippocampal place cells are organized to fire sequentially within individual cycles of theta oscillations (4–12 Hz) and form time-compressed representations of behavioral experiences, referred to as theta sequences.
source: In the context of active navigation in an environment, hippocampal place cells are organized to fire sequentially within individual cycles of theta oscillations (4–12 Hz) and form time-compressed representations of behavioral experiences, referred to as theta sequences (Colgin, 2020; Comrie et al., 2022; Dragoi and Buzsáki, 2006; Skaggs et al., 1996; Wallis, 2018).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous work (Colgin, 2020; Comrie et al., 2022; Dragoi and Buzsáki, 2006; Skaggs et al., 1996; Wallis, 2018).

claim: Theta sequences represent information about potential future paths that could guide goal-directed behaviors by sweeping ahead from the past to the upcoming locations.
source: By sweeping ahead from the past to the upcoming locations, theta sequences represent information about potential future paths that could guide goal-directed behaviors (Gupta et al., 2012; Joshi et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2021).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous work (Gupta et al., 2012; Joshi et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2021).

claim: Predictive theta sequences exhibited experience-dependent development when rats were exploring a novel environment or learning a novel goal location.
source: These predictive theta sequences exhibited experience-dependent development when rats were exploring a novel environment or learning a novel goal location (Feng et al., 2015; Gobbo et al., 2022; Wikenheiser and Redish, 2015; Zheng et al., 2021).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous work (Feng et al., 2015; Gobbo et al., 2022; Wikenheiser and Redish, 2015; Zheng et al., 2021).

claim: Theta sequences were manifestations of theta phase precession, in which an individual place cell fired at progressively earlier theta phase as the animal traversed the place field.
source: A common assumption was established by previous studies that theta sequences were manifestations of theta phase precession, in which an individual place cell fired at progressively earlier theta phase as the animal traversed the place field (Aoki et al., 2023; Foster and Wilson, 2007; O'Keefe and Recce, 1993; Qasim et al., 2021; Skaggs et al., 1996).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous work (Aoki et al., 2023; Foster and Wilson, 2007; O'Keefe and Recce, 1993; Qasim et al., 2021; Skaggs et al., 1996).

claim: The sequential structures of theta sequences were not developed on the first experience of a novel environment even if the phase precession of individual place cells has been observed.
source: However, when examined the theta sequences with experience at single trial level, their sequential structures were not developed on the first experience of a novel environment even if the phase precession of individual place cells has been observed (Colgin, 2020; Feng et al., 2015).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous work (Colgin, 2020; Feng et al., 2015).

claim: Fast and slow gamma rhythms occur at distinct theta phases and coordinate theta sequences in different manners.
source: As two subtypes of gamma, fast and slow gamma rhythms (Colgin et al., 2009; Schomburg et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2019) occur at distinct theta phases and coordinate theta sequences in different manners (Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous work (Colgin et al., 2009; Schomburg et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2016).

claim: Fast gamma (~65–100 Hz), associated with the input from the medial entorhinal cortex, is thought to rapidly encode ongoing novel information in the context.
source: Fast gamma (~65–100 Hz), associated with the input from the medial entorhinal cortex, is thought to rapidly encode ongoing novel information in the context (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2021; Kemere et al., 2013; Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous work (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2021; Kemere et al., 2013; Zheng et al., 2016).

claim: During fast gamma rhythms, place cell spikes occurred across all positions within a place field and displayed theta phase precession.
source: During fast gamma rhythms, place cell spikes occurred across all positions within a place field and displayed theta phase precession (Bieri et al., 2014).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to previous work (Bieri et al., 2014).

claim: Phase-precessing cells were identified recently, in which the phase-precession pattern emerges with strong fast gamma.
source: This type of cells was identified recently as 'phase-precessing' cells, in which the phase-precession pattern emerges with strong fast gamma (Guardamagna et al., 2023).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to previous work (Guardamagna et al., 2023).

claim: Slow gamma (~25–45 Hz) in the hippocampal CA1 reflects information received from CA3, which is responsible for the integration processing of learned information and experience.
source: Slow gamma (~25–45 Hz) in the hippocampal CA1 reflects information received from CA3, which is responsible for the integration processing of learned information and experience (Colgin et al., 2009; Zhu et al., 2023).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous work (Colgin et al., 2009; Zhu et al., 2023).

claim: Spiking during slow gamma exhibited dominant theta phase-locking and attenuated theta phase precession.
source: In contrast to fast gamma, spiking during slow gamma exhibited dominant theta phase-locking and attenuated theta phase precession (Guardamagna et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous work (Guardamagna et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2019).

claim: Place cells spiking exhibited slow gamma phase precession, to generate mini-sequences in an individual theta sequence, for highly time-compressed representation of ongoing and future information.
source: Place cells spiking exhibited slow gamma phase precession, to generate mini-sequences in an individual theta sequence, for highly time-compressed representation of ongoing and future information (Zheng et al., 2016; Zheng et al., 2021).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous work (Zheng et al., 2016; Zheng et al., 2021).

claim: 32% of hippocampal pyramidal cells were phase-locked to gamma rhythms during waking theta states.
source: As shown in a previous study, 32% of hippocampal pyramidal cells were phase-locked to gamma rhythms during waking theta states (Senior et al., 2008).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to previous work (Senior et al., 2008).

claim: Fast gamma episodes were detected with dominantly high probability as initial exploration of each day and decreased probability as being familiar to the environment.
source: Fast gamma episodes were detected with dominantly high probability as initial exploration of each day and decreased probability as being familiar to the environment (Bieri et al., 2014).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to previous work (Bieri et al., 2014).

claim: The information propagation of visual stimulation was unlikely synchronized between visual cortex and hippocampal CA1.
source: Although the information propagation of visual stimulation was unlikely synchronized between visual cortex and hippocampal CA1 (Schneider et al., 2023), the MEC inputs could also be entrained by fast gamma to process ongoing sensory information to the hippocampus (Buzsáki and Schomburg, 2015; Colgin et al., 2009).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous work (Schneider et al., 2023; Buzsáki and Schomburg, 2015; Colgin et al., 2009).

claim: The MEC inputs could be entrained by fast gamma to process ongoing sensory information to the hippocampus.
source: Although the information propagation of visual stimulation was unlikely synchronized between visual cortex and hippocampal CA1 (Schneider et al., 2023), the MEC inputs could also be entrained by fast gamma to process ongoing sensory information to the hippocampus (Buzsáki and Schomburg, 2015; Colgin et al., 2009).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous work (Buzsáki and Schomburg, 2015; Colgin et al., 2009).

claim: Optogenetically entraining the MEC GABAergic cells at an artificial gamma frequency (53 Hz) resulted in the loss of phase precession patterns in CA1 place cells and disrupted development of theta sequences.
source: Liu and colleagues optogenetically entrained the MEC GABAergic cells at an artificial gamma frequency (53 Hz) and observed the loss of phase precession patterns in CA1 place cells, and thereby the disrupted development of theta sequences (Liu et al., 2023).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to previous work (Liu et al., 2023).

claim: Fast gamma was found diminished between MEC and CA1 in transgenic model mice of Alzheimer's Disease, linked with spatial memory impairment in AD as a circuit mechanism.
source: Fast gamma was also found diminished between MEC and CA1 in transgenic model mice of Alzheimer's Disease, linked with spatial memory impairment in AD as a circuit mechanism (Jun et al., 2020).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to previous work (Jun et al., 2020).

claim: Fast gamma-dominated theta sequences represented shorter trajectories with relative less spatial information within a theta cycle.
source: On the other hand, our previous study showed that fast gamma-dominated theta sequences represented shorter trajectories with relative less spatial information within a theta cycle (Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to previous work (Zheng et al., 2016).

claim: Silencing of CA3 output did not affect theta phase precession of a single cell, but impaired theta sequence structures.
source: This finding was in line with a previous study showing that silencing of CA3 output did not affect theta phase precession of a single cell, but impaired theta sequence structures (Middleton and McHugh, 2016).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to previous work (Middleton and McHugh, 2016).

claim: Recruitment of PV-interneurons during the CA3-driven descending phase of the theta cycle, associated with the induction of slow gamma oscillations in CA1, was found reduced in the absence of CA3 input.
source: A possibility was that recruitment of PV-interneurons during the CA3-driven descending phase of the theta cycle, associated with the induction of slow gamma oscillations in CA1, was found reduced in the absence of CA3 input (Fernandez-Ruiz et al., 2023; Topolnik and Tamboli, 2022).
evidence: Directly stated with citations to previous work (Fernandez-Ruiz et al., 2023; Topolnik and Tamboli, 2022).

claim: The proportion of c-Fos-positive place cells (putative engram cells) had higher proportion being phase-locked to fast gamma than the c-Fos-negative place cells.
source: Indeed, the proportion of c-Fos-positive place cells (putative engram cells) had higher proportion being phase-locked to fast gamma than the c-Fos-negative place cells (Tanaka et al., 2018).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to previous work (Tanaka et al., 2018).

claim: FG-cells were largely overlapped with the previously defined 'fast-firing neurons', which remained stable during learning process.
source: Another possibility was that these FG-cells were largely overlapped with the previously defined 'fast-firing neurons', which remained stable during learning process (Grosmark and Buzsáki, 2016).
evidence: Directly stated with citation to previous work (Grosmark and Buzsáki, 2016).

claim: Rats ran five trials (laps) on the circular track in each recording day (session).
source: In each recording day (session), rats ran five trials (or laps) on the track (inner diameter of 90 cm, height of 50 cm, and width of 10 cm, surrounded by a blue curtain) without receiving any food reward.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing the behavioral paradigm.

claim: Multi-tetrode drives containing 21 independently moveable tetrodes (18 recording tetrodes and 3 reference tetrodes) were implanted into the hippocampal dorsal CA1 region.
source: Multi-tetrode drives containing 21 independently moveable tetrodes (18 recording tetrodes and 3 reference tetrodes) were implanted into the hippocampal dorsal CA1 region (anterior–posterior [AP] –3.5 mm, medial–lateral [ML] 3.0 mm, dorsal–ventral [DV] 1 mm on day of implantation).
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing surgery and tetrode implanting.

claim: LFPs from one channel within each tetrode were continuously recorded in the 0.1–500 Hz band at a 2,000 Hz sampling rate.
source: LFPs from one channel within each tetrode were continuously recorded in the 0.1–500 Hz band at a 2,000 Hz sampling rate.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing data acquisition.

claim: To detect unit activity, signals from each channel in a tetrode were bandpass filtered from 600 to 6000 Hz.
source: To detect unit activity, signals from each channel in a tetrode were bandpass filtered from 600 to 6000 Hz.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing data acquisition.

claim: The spike was detected when the signal on one or more of the channels exceeded a threshold set at 55 μV.
source: The spike was detected when the signal on one or more of the channels exceeded a threshold set at 55 μV.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing data acquisition.

claim: The video was recorded through the Neuralynx system with a resolution of 720 × 480 pixels and a frame rate of 25 frames per second.
source: The video was recorded through the Neuralynx system with a resolution of 720 × 480 pixels and a frame rate of 25 frames per second.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing data acquisition.

claim: Detected spikes that occurred during trials were manually sorted using graphical cluster-cutting software (MClust).
source: Detected spikes that occurred during trials were manually sorted using graphical cluster-cutting software (MClust; A.D. Redish, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis).
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing spike sorting.

claim: Units with mean firing rates that were higher than 15 Hz were identified as putative fast-spiking interneurons and were excluded.
source: Units with mean firing rates that were higher than 15 Hz were identified as putative fast-spiking interneurons and were excluded.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing spike sorting.

claim: Only units with peak firing rates over 1 Hz and main field size over 3 angle bins (approximately 10.5 cm) during trials were defined as putative neurons with spatial representation.
source: Only units with peak firing rates over 1 Hz and main field size over 3 angle bins (approximately 10.5 cm) during trials were defined as putative neurons with spatial representation.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing spike sorting.

claim: A putative excitatory neuron, which at least had one place field, was defined as a place cell.
source: A putative excitatory neuron, which at least had one place field, was defined as a place cell.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing spike sorting.

claim: Time-varying power for slow gamma and fast gamma was computed, using a Morlet's wavelet transform method.
source: Time-varying power for slow gamma and fast gamma was computed, using a Morlet's wavelet transform method described previously (Tallon-Baudry et al., 1997; Zheng et al., 2016), and then averaged within each frequency range.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing detection of gamma episodes, with citations to previous work (Tallon-Baudry et al., 1997; Zheng et al., 2016).

claim: The timestamp of z-scored time-varying power ≥3 was set as the center of a slow or fast gamma episode, and a 160-ms window around this center was defined as a gamma episode.
source: To detect slow and fast gamma episodes, we z-scored the time-varying power for slow and fast gamma across time within each trial. The timestamp of z-scored time-varying power ≥3 was set as the center of a slow or fast gamma episode, and a 160-ms window around this center was defined as a gamma episode.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing detection of gamma episodes.

claim: Significant phase-locking to either slow or fast gamma was detected by Rayleigh test on phase distributions with at least 10 spikes in each lap.
source: Significant phase-locking to either slow or fast gamma was detected by Rayleigh test on phase distributions with at least 10 spikes in each lap.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing detection of FG- and NFG-cells.

claim: Theta phase precession was examined in linearized spatial turning curves using a circular-linear fit.
source: Theta phase precession was examined in linearized spatial turning curves (see Spike sorting and turning curve analysis). For spikes within each place field, phase precession was computed using a circular-linear fit (Kempter et al., 2012).
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing theta phase precession, with citation to previous work (Kempter et al., 2012).

claim: For each trial, a memoryless Bayesian decoder was built at 90 angle bins (ranging from 0 to 2pi) by using spikes during locomotion (running speed >5 cm/s) in this trial.
source: For each trial, a memoryless Bayesian decoder was built at 90 angle bins (ranging from 0 to 2pi) by using spikes during locomotion (running speed >5 cm/s) in this trial.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing single-trial Bayesian decoding analysis.

claim: Decoding was performed using a 20-ms sliding time window with 5-ms stepping.
source: Decoding was performed using a 20-ms sliding time window with 5-ms stepping.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing single-trial Bayesian decoding analysis.

claim: Theta rhythms were detected from a central tetrode of all recording tetrodes which located in the stratum pyramidale of hippocampus.
source: Theta rhythms were detected from a central tetrode of all recording tetrodes which located in the stratum pyramidale of hippocampus.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing theta sequences detection.

claim: Raw theta sequences were detected by the following criteria: (1) during the sequence, the animal was running between the starting point and ending point of the track, with running speed higher than 5 cm/s; (2) the duration of the sequence ranged from 100 to 200 ms; (3) more than 3 place cells which emitted at least 5 spikes within each sequence.
source: Raw theta sequences were detected by the following criteria: (1) during the sequence, the animal was running between the starting point and ending point of the track, with running speed higher than 5 cm/s; (2) the duration of the sequence ranged from 100 to 200 ms; (3) more than 3 place cells which emitted at least 5 spikes within each sequence.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing theta sequences detection.

claim: Weighted correlation of each theta sequence was calculated from the decoded probabilities of positions 35 cm behind and ahead of the rat's current location, in a time window of ±30 ms (approximate 1⁄4 theta cycle) before and after the mid-time point of each theta sequence.
source: Weighted correlation of each theta sequence was calculated from the decoded probabilities of positions 35 cm behind and ahead of the rat's current location, in a time window of ±30 ms (approximate 1⁄4 theta cycle) before and after the mid-time point of each theta sequence (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing weighted correlation of theta sequences, with reference to Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The gamma cycle with maximal spiking across all simultaneously recorded cells was defined as cycle 0.
source: The gamma cycle with maximal spiking across all simultaneously recorded cells was defined as cycle 0.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing slow gamma phase shift analysis of cell ensemble.

claim: The theta cycle with z-scored time varying power ≥1.5 was defined as slow gamma events.
source: To identify the theta cycle with high slow gamma power, we z-scored time-varying slow gamma power across the theta cycle within each trial. The theta cycle with z-scored time varying power ≥1.5 was defined as slow gamma events.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing slow gamma phase shift analysis of individual cell.

claim: A negative slow gamma phase difference value indicates phase precession, while a positive value indicates phase procession.
source: A negative slow gamma phase difference value indicates phase precession, while a positive value indicates phase procession.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing slow gamma phase shift analysis of individual cell.

claim: FG-cells exhibited slow gamma phase precession within theta cycles associated with the sweep-ahead structure of theta sequences, which occurred earlier than those cells not phase-locked to fast gamma (NFG-cells).
source: Furthermore, these cells exhibited slow gamma phase precession within theta cycles associated with the sweep-ahead structure of theta sequences, which occurred earlier than those cells not phase-locked to fast gamma (NFG-cells).

source: These findings highlight the dynamic network modulation by fast and slow gamma in the development of theta sequences which may further facilitate memory encoding and retrieval.
